front: What is the only difference between struct and class in C++, and what does that mean for a Python-fluent quant reading a pricer's headers?
back:
Answer: Default member access and default inheritance. A struct is public by default, a class is private by default. Otherwise both can have constructors, methods, virtual functions, templates and private members.
Convention: struct for passive data, class for a type with an invariant. The language does not enforce it.
#include <iostream>

struct Point { int x; int y; };          // members are public by default

class Secret {                            // members are private by default
    int v = 0;
public:
    void set(int a) { v = a; }
    int get() const { return v; }
};

int main() {
    Point p{3, 4};
    Secret s;
    s.set(7);
    std::cout << p.x + p.y << ' ' << s.get() << '\n';
}
Output:
7 7

Compile check for private access:g++ says:
snippet.cpp:9:17: error: ‘int Secret::v’ is private within this context

Interview trap: struct does not mean plain-old-data. A struct can have a constructor, private members and virtual functions.

front: A constructor's member initializer list is written in a different order from the member declarations. Does it compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, what does it print, and what is the real rule?
back:
Answer: Members are initialised in declaration order, whatever order the initializer list uses. g++ warns with -Wreorder (enabled by -Wall) but still compiles.
#include <iostream>

struct Bond {
    double face;
    double price;
    double yield;                       // declared last

    Bond(double f, double p)
        : yield((f - p) / p),           // listed first, initialised last
          price(p),
          face(f)                       // listed last, initialised first
    {
        std::cout << "face=" << face << " price=" << price
                  << " yield=" << yield << '\n';
    }
};

int main() { Bond b(100.0, 98.0); }
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:6:12: warning: ‘Bond::yield’ will be initialized after [-Wreorder]
snippet.cpp:5:12: warning:   ‘double Bond::price’ [-Wreorder]
Output:
face=100 price=98 yield=0.0204082
Interview trap: here yield is computed from the parameters, so the output is correct. If it had read price, a member declared earlier but initialised later, it would have read an uninitialised value. The warning is the only hint, and nothing guarantees a diagnostic for that read.

front: A {{c1::reference}} or {{c2::const}} member cannot be assigned in the constructor body, so it must be set in the member initializer list. All members are initialised {{c3::before}} the constructor body runs.
What is RAII in C++, and what is the closest Python construct? Name the guarantee Python does not give you for the same pattern.
back:
Answer: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. The constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it. The object's lifetime, which follows the scope, controls the release, including when an exception unwinds the stack.
Python's closest equivalent is the context manager (with). It is deterministic only if the caller remembers to write with. The C++ release is part of the type, so the caller cannot forget it.
#include <iostream>

struct Guard {
    const char* name;
    explicit Guard(const char* n) : name(n) { std::cout << "acquire " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Guard() { std::cout << "release " << name << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "start\n";
    {
        Guard g("db-connection");
        std::cout << "work\n";
    }                                  // destructor runs here, every time
    std::cout << "end\n";
}
Output:
start
acquire db-connection
work
release db-connection
end
Interview trap: RAII is a property of the type. A local object of a class with a releasing destructor is safe with no caller discipline.

front: Python's __del__ has no guaranteed timing: CPython calls it when the {{c1::reference count drops to zero}}, and other implementations may call it much later. A C++ destructor runs {{c2::at scope exit, deterministically}}.
back:
#include <iostream>

struct Guard {
    const char* name;
    explicit Guard(const char* n) : name(n) { std::cout << "acquire " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Guard() { std::cout << "release " << name << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "start\n";
    {
        Guard g("db-connection");
        std::cout << "work\n";
    }                                  // destructor runs here, every time
    std::cout << "end\n";
}
Output:
start
acquire db-connection
work
release db-connection
end
Interview trap: do not rely on __del__ to release a lock or close a file. The C++ equivalents are std::lock_guard and std::unique_ptr.

front: What does this program print, and in what order do the destructors run? State the rule for the containing object's destructor body and its members.
back:
Answer: The constructor runs members first (in declaration order), then the constructor body. On scope exit the destructor body runs first, then the members are destroyed in reverse declaration order. Base classes are destroyed after the derived destructor body and their members are destroyed in reverse order too.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Tag {
    std::string name;
    Tag(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::cout << "ctor " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Tag() { std::cout << "dtor " << name << '\n'; }
};

struct Position {
    Tag first{"first-member"};
    Tag second{"second-member"};
    ~Position() { std::cout << "dtor Position\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Position p;
    std::cout << "body\n";
}
Output:
ctor first-member
ctor second-member
body
dtor Position
dtor second-member
dtor first-member
Interview trap: the reverse order follows the declaration order, not the order of the mem-initializer list (see the earlier init-order card for that).

front: This class owns a raw array with a destructor but declares no copy operations. What is wrong with Buffer b = a;, and what does AddressSanitizer report when the program runs?
back:
Answer: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer member-wise. Both objects then run delete[] on the same array. That is a double free, undefined behaviour.
g++ with -Wall -Wextra does not warn, so the bug is silent at compile time. Compiled with -fsanitize=address, the first line of the report is:
#include <cstddef>

class Buffer {
    double* data_;
    std::size_t n_;
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(new double[n]()), n_(n) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }
    // no copy operations declared: the compiler generates a member-wise copy
    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
};

int main() {
    Buffer a(4);
    Buffer b = a;                       // both objects now hold the same pointer
    return static_cast<int>(a.size() + b.size()) - 8;
}

==4662==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free on 0x503000000040 in thread T0:
Fix: a deep copy (rule of three), or = delete the copy operations and implement a move (rule of five).
Interview trap: the implicit copy is the default that bites: a class holding a raw resource must say what copying means.

front: State the rule of zero, the rule of three and the rule of five. Which one should a class whose only members are std::string and std::vector follow, and why?
back:
Answer:
  • Rule of zero: declare no special member functions when every member manages its own resource. The compiler generates correct copy, move and destructor code.
  • Rule of three: if you write a destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three.
  • Rule of five: the rule of three plus the move constructor and move assignment.
The rule of zero is the default. Here the class follows it, so the compiler writes deep copies and moves for you.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Ladder {                         // rule of zero: no special members declared
    std::string name;
    std::vector<double> pillars;
};

int main() {
    Ladder a{"USD-SOFR", {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}};
    Ladder b = a;                       // deep copy, generated by the compiler
    b.pillars.push_back(5.0);
    b.name = "EUR";
    std::cout << a.name << ' ' << a.pillars.size() << '\n';
    std::cout << b.name << ' ' << b.pillars.size() << '\n';
    Ladder c = std::move(b);            // move generated too
    std::cout << c.name << ' ' << c.pillars.size() << '\n';
}
Output:
USD-SOFR 3
EUR 4
EUR 4
Interview trap: declaring a move constructor deletes the implicit copy constructor. A class with only a move constructor becomes move-only without warning. Declaring a destructor suppresses the implicit move (next card).

front: A user-declared destructor {{c1::suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment}}, so a move falls back to {{c2::copy}}. The implicit copy operations are still generated, but deprecated.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

struct Noisy {
    Noisy() { std::cout << "default\n"; }
    Noisy(const Noisy&) { std::cout << "copy\n"; }
    Noisy(Noisy&&) noexcept { std::cout << "move\n"; }
    ~Noisy() = default;
};

struct NoDtor { Noisy n; };             // implicit move constructor is generated

struct WithDtor {                       // user-declared destructor
    Noisy n;
    ~WithDtor() {}
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "-- NoDtor\n";
    NoDtor a;
    NoDtor a2 = std::move(a);
    std::cout << "-- WithDtor\n";
    WithDtor b;
    WithDtor b2 = std::move(b);         // no implicit move: falls back to copy
    (void)a2; (void)b2;
}
Output:
-- NoDtor
default
move
-- WithDtor
default
copy
Interview trap: ~X() = default; counts as user-declared and also suppresses the implicit move. Declare the moves explicitly with = default, or follow the rule of zero.

front: Implement a Buffer that owns a heap array under the rule of five. Show the copy-and-swap assignment, and explain why the move operations are noexcept.
back:
Answer: The copy constructor allocates and copies. Copy assignment builds a temporary copy and swaps it in, which gives the strong exception guarantee and handles self-assignment. The move constructor steals the pointer and nulls the source. Move assignment releases the old array first and then steals. The moves never allocate, so they are noexcept.
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

class Buffer {
    double* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t n_ = 0;
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(new double[n]()), n_(n) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }

    Buffer(const Buffer& o) : data_(new double[o.n_]), n_(o.n_) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) data_[i] = o.data_[i];
    }
    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& o) {
        if (this != &o) { Buffer tmp(o); swap(tmp); }   // copy-and-swap
        return *this;
    }
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept
        : data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)), n_(std::exchange(o.n_, 0)) {}
    Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            delete[] data_;
            data_ = std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr);
            n_ = std::exchange(o.n_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }
    void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept { std::swap(data_, o.data_); std::swap(n_, o.n_); }
    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
};

int main() {
    Buffer a(3);
    Buffer b = a;                       // deep copy
    Buffer c = std::move(a);            // steal the pointer, leave a empty
    std::cout << "a=" << a.size() << " b=" << b.size() << " c=" << c.size() << '\n';
    b = std::move(c);
    std::cout << "b=" << b.size() << '\n';
}
Output:
a=0 b=3 c=3
b=3
Interview trap: std::exchange leaves the moved-from object in a valid state (null pointer, size 0). That is what makes its destructor and assignment safe. A moved-from object is not required to be empty, only destructible and assignable.

front: Two element types differ only in whether their move constructor is noexcept. What does std::vector do on reallocation with each type, and what counts does this program print?
back:
Answer: On growth, std::vector moves the elements only if the move constructor is noexcept, or if no copy constructor exists. Otherwise it copies them, to keep the strong exception guarantee.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Fast {
    Fast() = default;
    Fast(const Fast&) { ++copies; }
    Fast(Fast&&) noexcept { ++moves; }
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
};

struct Slow {
    Slow() = default;
    Slow(const Slow&) { ++copies; }
    Slow(Slow&&) { ++moves; }           // not noexcept
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Fast> f;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) f.push_back(Fast{});
    std::cout << "Fast: copies=" << Fast::copies << " moves=" << Fast::moves << '\n';

    std::vector<Slow> s;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) s.push_back(Slow{});
    std::cout << "Slow: copies=" << Slow::copies << " moves=" << Slow::moves << '\n';
}
Output:
Fast: copies=0 moves=6
Slow: copies=3 moves=3
The count is for libstdc++, which grows capacity 1, 2, 4. Three pushes cause two reallocations. The standard does not fix the growth sequence, so do not rely on the exact counts.
Interview trap: a non-noexcept move in a hot container type silently turns every growth into a deep copy. std::string and std::vector have noexcept moves for this reason.

front: Python's b = a aliases a list, while auto b = a; on a std::vector copies it. What is the C++ equivalent of aliasing, and what does this program print?
back:
Answer: Value semantics are the default in C++. A copy is a deep copy of the whole container. Aliasing needs a reference, &, which is what Python's b = a gives you by default.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> a{1.0, 2.0};
    auto b = a;                          // deep copy: unlike Python's b = a[:] it is the default
    b[0] = 99.0;
    std::cout << a[0] << ' ' << b[0] << '\n';
    std::vector<double>& alias = a;      // a reference is what Python's b = a gives you
    alias[1] = 7.0;
    std::cout << a[1] << '\n';
}
Output:
1 99
7
Interview trap: a function taking std::vector<double> by value copies the whole vector on every call. In a pricing loop that is a silent O(n) per call. Pass const std::vector<double>&.

front: What does mutable allow inside a const member function, and what does this program print? Why is the cache keyed on t?
back:
Answer: Inside a const member function this is const Curve*, so ordinary members cannot change. mutable members can, which is how a lazy cache fits in a logically constant method. The cache is keyed on t, so a call with a different t recomputes and does not return a stale value.
#include <iostream>

class Curve {
    double rate_;
    mutable double cached_df_ = 0.0;     // may change inside a const member function
    mutable double cached_t_ = -1.0;
public:
    explicit Curve(double r) : rate_(r) {}
    double df(double t) const {
        if (t != cached_t_) {
            cached_df_ = 1.0 / (1.0 + rate_ * t);
            cached_t_ = t;
        }
        return cached_df_;
    }
    void set_rate(double r) { rate_ = r; cached_t_ = -1.0; }
};

int main() {
    const Curve c(0.05);
    std::cout << c.df(2.0) << ' ' << c.df(2.0) << ' ' << c.df(4.0) << '\n';
}
Output:
0.909091 0.909091 0.833333
Interview trap: const means the logical value does not change, not that the call is thread-safe. Two threads calling df at once race on cached_t_ and cached_df_. Guard the cache with a mutex, or compute it outside the class.

front: What does explicit on a single-argument constructor prevent, and why does Notional n{100.0}; still compile?
back:
Answer: explicit blocks implicit conversions: copy-initialisation, passing an argument to a function, returning a value. Direct-list-initialisation and direct-initialisation are still allowed.
#include <iostream>

struct Notional {
    double amount;
    explicit Notional(double a) : amount(a) {}
};

double pv_scaled(Notional n, double df) { return n.amount * df; }

int main() {
    Notional n{100.0};                   // direct-list-initialisation: fine
    std::cout << pv_scaled(n, 0.95) << '\n';
    // pv_scaled(100.0, 0.95);           // not allowed: explicit blocks the conversion
}
Output:
95
Without the conversion, the compiler rejects the commented-out call:
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:8:48: error: could not convert ‘1.0e+2’ from ‘double’ to ‘Notional’
Interview trap: explicit does not stop Notional n(100.0), which is direct-initialisation. It only blocks the implicit conversions.

front: A non-explicit single-argument constructor is an implicit {{c1::conversion}}. Passing 100.0 to a function taking Notional {{c2::silently builds a temporary Notional}}.
back:
#include <iostream>

struct Notional {
    double amount;
    Notional(double a) : amount(a) {}    // no explicit
};

double pv_scaled(Notional n, double df) { return n.amount * df; }

int main() {
    std::cout << pv_scaled(100.0, 0.95) << '\n';   // double silently converted
}
Output:
95
Interview trap: one user-defined conversion is allowed per implicit conversion. A chain of two user-defined conversions does not compile.

front: What is a static data member in C++, how does it differ from a Python class attribute, and what does this program print?
back:
Answer: One variable per class, shared by all its objects, much like a Python class attribute. Since C++17, inline static gives it a definition inside the class. Here it counts live Trade objects.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class Trade {
public:
    inline static int live_count = 0;          // one object shared by all instances (C++17)
    static int created() { return live_count; } // no this pointer
    std::string id;
    explicit Trade(std::string s) : id(std::move(s)) { ++live_count; }
    ~Trade() { --live_count; }
};

int main() {
    Trade a{"T1"};
    {
        Trade b{"T2"};
        std::cout << Trade::live_count << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << Trade::created() << ' ' << a.live_count << '\n';
}
Output:
2
1 1
Interview trap: static objects in different translation units are initialised in unspecified order (the static initialisation order fiasco). Do not let one global's constructor read another global from a different .cpp.

front: A static member function has {{c1::no this pointer}}, so it cannot touch non-static members. Since C++17, an inline static data member is {{c2::defined in the class}} and needs no out-of-class definition.
Why is operator+ usually a free function that takes its first argument by value, while operator+= is a member? Use the Money example and state the output.
back:
Answer: += changes the left operand, so it is a member returning a reference to it. + does not change either operand. Taking the left operand by value and reusing += keeps the two operators consistent with one implementation.
#include <iostream>

class Money {
public:
    double amt;
    explicit Money(double a) : amt(a) {}
    Money& operator+=(const Money& o) { amt += o.amt; return *this; }   // member
};

Money operator+(Money a, const Money& b) { a += b; return a; }          // free function
Money operator*(double k, const Money& m) { return Money(k * m.amt); }  // double on the left
Money operator*(const Money& m, double k) { return Money(k * m.amt); }

int main() {
    Money a{100.0}, b{25.5};
    Money c = a + b;
    Money d = 2.0 * c;
    Money e = d * 0.5;
    std::cout << c.amt << ' ' << d.amt << ' ' << e.amt << '\n';
}
Output:
125.5 251 125.5
Interview trap: 2.0 * m needs a free function. A member operator requires the left operand to be the class type, and a double cannot be one.

front: In Python, 2.0 * m calls float.__mul__, which returns NotImplemented, and then Money.__rmul__. How does C++ handle the same expression, and what does it print?
back:
Answer: There is no runtime fallback chain. Overload resolution looks for an operator* whose parameters match (double, Money). A free function declares that signature directly.
#include <iostream>

class Money {
public:
    double amt;
    explicit Money(double a) : amt(a) {}
    Money& operator+=(const Money& o) { amt += o.amt; return *this; }   // member
};

Money operator+(Money a, const Money& b) { a += b; return a; }          // free function
Money operator*(double k, const Money& m) { return Money(k * m.amt); }  // double on the left
Money operator*(const Money& m, double k) { return Money(k * m.amt); }

int main() {
    Money a{100.0}, b{25.5};
    Money c = a + b;
    Money d = 2.0 * c;
    Money e = d * 0.5;
    std::cout << c.amt << ' ' << d.amt << ' ' << e.amt << '\n';
}
Output:
125.5 251 125.5
Interview trap: an operator overload set cannot be patched at runtime the way Python method lookup can. The matching overload is chosen at compile time.

front: A class declares auto operator<=>(const Tenor&) const = default; and nothing else. Does a == b compile? What happens if you write <=> by hand?
back:
Answer: A defaulted <=> implicitly declares a defaulted ==, so this compiles. It compares member by member and generates <, <=, >, >=. A hand-written <=> does not get an implicit ==, so == fails.
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Tenor {
    int months;
    auto operator<=>(const Tenor&) const = default;   // defaulted: also implicitly declares ==
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Tenor> v{{12}, {3}, {6}};
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    for (auto t : v) std::cout << t.months << ' ';
    std::cout << (Tenor{6} < Tenor{12}) << ' ' << (Tenor{3} == Tenor{3}) << '\n';
}
Output:
3 6 12 1 1
Hand-written version, without ==:
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:8:30: error: no match for ‘operator==’ (operand types are ‘Tenor’ and ‘Tenor’)
Interview trap: a defaulted <=> over a double member returns std::partial_ordering, not strong_ordering, because NaN is unordered. NaN breaks the strict weak ordering that std::sort needs, so sorting data that contains NaN is undefined behaviour.

front: What is a function object (functor) in C++, and which Python construct does it correspond to? State the output of this program that passes one to std::transform.
back:
Answer: A class with operator(). It corresponds to a Python object with __call__. It can hold state (here the strike) and is passed to standard algorithms.
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>

struct EuropeanCall {
    double strike;
    double operator()(double spot) const { return spot > strike ? spot - strike : 0.0; }
};

int main() {
    EuropeanCall call{100.0};
    std::vector<double> spots{90.0, 100.0, 115.0};
    std::vector<double> pays;
    std::transform(spots.begin(), spots.end(), std::back_inserter(pays), call);
    for (double p : pays) std::cout << p << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n' << call(120.0) << '\n';
}
Output:
0 0 15 
20
Interview trap: a plain functor type is inlined by the compiler. std::function erases the type and calls indirectly, which costs more inside a hot loop.

front: [Chain: Virtual 1/3] Context: a vector<unique_ptr<Instrument>> holds a Bond and a Swap, and the loop calls i->pv(). Which function runs, and what makes that decision at runtime?
back:
Answer: The derived override runs. Each object carries a hidden vptr to its class's vtable. The call loads the vptr, reads the function slot for pv, and jumps there. This is dynamic dispatch.
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Instrument {
    virtual ~Instrument() = default;
    virtual double pv() const = 0;
    virtual const char* name() const { return "Instrument"; }
};

struct Bond : Instrument {
    double pv() const override { return 98.5; }
    const char* name() const override { return "Bond"; }
};

struct Swap : Instrument {
    double pv() const override { return -1.25; }
    const char* name() const override { return "Swap"; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Instrument>> book;
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<Bond>());
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<Swap>());
    for (const auto& i : book)
        std::cout << i->name() << ' ' << i->pv() << '\n';
}
Output:
Bond 98.5
Swap -1.25
Interview trap: the cost is an extra pointer load and an indirect branch. It also blocks inlining at that call site unless the compiler can devirtualise it.

front: [Chain: Virtual 2/3] Context: the same instrument hierarchy, now looking at object size. What does adding a virtual function do to sizeof? Predict the four numbers before reading the output.
back:
Answer: A class with virtual functions holds a vptr, 8 bytes on x86-64 with g++. Struct A has no virtual and is 4 bytes. B has a vptr, an int, and 4 bytes of padding, so 16. C is just the vptr, 8. D has no vptr, a double and an int padded to 16.
#include <iostream>

struct A { int x; };
struct B { virtual void f() {} int x; };
struct C { virtual void f() {} };
struct D { double a; int b; };

int main() {
    std::cout << sizeof(A) << ' ' << sizeof(B) << ' ' << sizeof(C) << ' ' << sizeof(D) << '\n';
}
Output:
4 16 8 16
Interview trap: a polymorphic object cannot be stored by value in a vector<Base> without losing its derived behaviour. The next card shows the slicing.

front: [Chain: Virtual 3/3] Context: Base has a virtual function but a non-virtual destructor, and Derived owns a std::vector. What does delete p; on a Base* that points to a Derived do, and what does -Wall report?
back:
Answer: It is undefined behaviour. In this run only ~Base runs, so ~Derived never runs and the vector's heap block leaks. g++ warns:
warning: deleting object of polymorphic class type ‘Base’ which has non-virtual destructor might cause undefined behavior [-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor]
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Base {
    virtual double pv() const { return 0.0; }
    ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base\n"; }        // not virtual
};

struct Derived : Base {
    std::vector<double> curve{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
    ~Derived() { std::cout << "~Derived\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Base* p = new Derived;
    delete p;                                 // undefined behaviour
}
Output:
~Base
Fixed by making the base destructor virtual. Output of the fixed version, checked with AddressSanitizer for leaks, has no leak report:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Base {
    virtual double pv() const { return 0.0; }
    virtual ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base\n"; }   // virtual: the derived dtor runs too
};

struct Derived : Base {
    std::vector<double> curve{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
    ~Derived() override { std::cout << "~Derived\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Base* p = new Derived;
    delete p;
}
Output:
~Derived
~Base
Interview trap: a class meant to be deleted through a base pointer needs a virtual destructor. A protected non-virtual destructor is the way to forbid that delete.

front: A class with at least one virtual function holds a hidden {{c1::vptr}} to its class's {{c2::vtable}}. The vtable is one per class, shared by all objects. On x86-64 with g++ the vptr adds {{c3::8 bytes}} to the object.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Instrument {
    virtual ~Instrument() = default;
    virtual double pv() const = 0;
    virtual const char* name() const { return "Instrument"; }
};

struct Bond : Instrument {
    double pv() const override { return 98.5; }
    const char* name() const override { return "Bond"; }
};

struct Swap : Instrument {
    double pv() const override { return -1.25; }
    const char* name() const override { return "Swap"; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Instrument>> book;
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<Bond>());
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<Swap>());
    for (const auto& i : book)
        std::cout << i->name() << ' ' << i->pv() << '\n';
}
Output:
Bond 98.5
Swap -1.25
Calls through a base pointer read the vptr and index the vtable. Every object of the same dynamic type shares the same vtable.
Interview trap: the vptr is set by each constructor in turn, so during a base constructor it points to the base vtable (see the constructor card).

front: What is object slicing, and what does this program print for Base sliced = d;, show_by_value(d) and show_by_ref(d)?
back:
Answer: Copying a derived object into a base object copies only the base subobject. The extra member is lost, and the vptr is reset to Base, so virtual calls resolve to Base. Passing by reference keeps the object whole.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Base {
    int id = 1;
    virtual ~Base() = default;
    virtual std::string kind() const { return "Base"; }
};

struct Derived : Base {
    int extra = 42;
    std::string kind() const override { return "Derived"; }
};

void show_by_value(Base b) { std::cout << b.kind() << ' ' << b.id << '\n'; }
void show_by_ref(const Base& b) { std::cout << b.kind() << ' ' << b.id << '\n'; }

int main() {
    Derived d;
    Base sliced = d;                     // copy-initialisation slices off `extra`
    std::cout << sliced.kind() << '\n';
    show_by_value(d);
    show_by_ref(d);
}
Output:
Base
Base 1
Derived 1
Interview trap: std::vector<Base> filled with Derived objects is sliced on every push_back. A Python list keeps the subclass because it stores references. Store unique_ptr<Base> instead.

front: What makes a C++ class abstract, and what does the compiler say when you try to create an object of one? Show the message.
back:
Answer: At least one pure virtual function, declared = 0. An abstract class cannot be instantiated. You can hold it by pointer or reference, and a pure virtual may still have a body, callable with a qualified name.
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:7:12: error: cannot declare variable ‘p’ to be of abstract type ‘Payoff’
Interview trap: a derived class that misses one pure virtual (for example through a typo in the signature) stays abstract. The error appears only where that class is instantiated.

front: What do override and final each guarantee to the compiler? Show the two diagnostics this code triggers.
back:
Answer: override asks the compiler to check that the function really overrides a base virtual, so a mismatch in the signature is an error. final on a function forbids further overriding; final on a class forbids deriving from it. A class-level final lets the compiler devirtualise calls on objects of that exact type.
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:7:12: error: ‘double Mistake::pv(double)’ marked ‘override’, but does not override
snippet.cpp:2:20: warning: ‘virtual double Base::pv(double) const’ was hidden [-Woverloaded-virtual=]
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:10:8: error: cannot derive from ‘final’ base ‘Derived’ in derived type ‘Further’
Valid use, output:
#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    virtual double pv(double r) const { return r; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};

struct Derived final : Base {
    double pv(double r) const override { return 2.0 * r; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    const Base& b = d;
    std::cout << b.pv(5.0) << '\n';
}
Output:
10
Interview trap: the -Woverloaded-virtual warning in the first diagnostic is the clue. Without override the mismatched function would silently create a new overload, and calls through the base would still run the base version.

front: What does this program print? Explain why the default argument is taken from the static type, not the dynamic type.
back:
Answer: 10 20. Default arguments are bound at compile time from the static type of the expression. Virtual dispatch selects the function body at runtime, but the default is already fixed by the static type, here Model for ref.
#include <iostream>

struct Model {
    virtual double price(double vol = 0.10) const { return vol * 100.0; }
    virtual ~Model() = default;
};

struct Lognormal : Model {
    double price(double vol = 0.20) const override { return vol * 100.0; }
};

int main() {
    Lognormal m;
    Model& ref = m;
    std::cout << ref.price() << ' ' << m.price() << '\n';
}
Output:
10 20
Interview trap: defaults on virtual functions are a known source of wrong results. Keep them identical through the hierarchy, or omit them on virtuals.

front: What does calling a virtual function from a constructor do in C++? Predict the three lines this program prints.
back:
Answer: During Base's constructor the object's dynamic type is Base, so the vptr points to the base vtable and name() returns the base version. The derived part does not exist yet. The same happens in a destructor, where the derived part is already gone.
#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    Base() { std::cout << "Base ctor sees: " << name() << '\n'; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
    virtual const char* name() const { return "Base"; }
};

struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() { std::cout << "Derived ctor sees: " << name() << '\n'; }
    const char* name() const override { return "Derived"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    std::cout << d.name() << '\n';
}
Output:
Base ctor sees: Base
Derived ctor sees: Derived
Derived
Interview trap: a pure virtual called from a constructor or destructor is a runtime error. Do not put polymorphic initialisation in a constructor. Use a factory or an explicit init() call.

front: Pricer design: should a Swap inherit from a Leg class, or contain two Leg objects? State the rule and the cost of each choice.
back:
Answer: Prefer composition (has-a). Use inheritance (is-a) only when the derived type is substitutable for the base everywhere the base is used. A Swap is not a Leg, so it owns a fixed leg and a floating leg.
#include <iostream>

struct Leg {
    double notional;
    double rate;
};

struct Swap {                       // composition: a swap HAS two legs, it is not a kind of leg
    Leg fixed;
    Leg floating;
    double net_notional() const { return fixed.notional - floating.notional; }
};

int main() {
    Swap s{{100.0, 0.03}, {100.0, 0.025}};
    std::cout << s.fixed.rate - s.floating.rate << ' ' << s.net_notional() << '\n';
}
Output:
0.005 0
Interview trap: public inheritance from a concrete class makes the base's interface part of the derived type's contract. A Swap that derives from Leg can be passed where a Leg is expected, which is almost never meaningful.

front: Design a payoff hierarchy for a Monte Carlo pricer: an abstract base, a European call and put, a digital, and a straddle built from a call and a put by composition. Show the code and the payoffs at S=90 and S=110 for K=100.
back:
Answer: The base is an abstract interface with a pure virtual operator() and a virtual destructor, so unique_ptr<Payoff> deletes the right type. The straddle has-a call and has-a put.
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

class Payoff {
public:
    virtual ~Payoff() = default;
    virtual double operator()(double spot) const = 0;      // abstract interface
};

class EuropeanCall final : public Payoff {
    double k_;
public:
    explicit EuropeanCall(double k) : k_(k) {}
    double operator()(double s) const override { return std::max(s - k_, 0.0); }
};

class EuropeanPut final : public Payoff {
    double k_;
public:
    explicit EuropeanPut(double k) : k_(k) {}
    double operator()(double s) const override { return std::max(k_ - s, 0.0); }
};

class DigitalCall final : public Payoff {
    double k_, cash_;
public:
    DigitalCall(double k, double cash) : k_(k), cash_(cash) {}
    double operator()(double s) const override { return s > k_ ? cash_ : 0.0; }
};

class Straddle final : public Payoff {               // composition of two legs
    EuropeanCall call_;
    EuropeanPut put_;
public:
    explicit Straddle(double k) : call_(k), put_(k) {}
    double operator()(double s) const override { return call_(s) + put_(s); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Payoff>> book;
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<EuropeanCall>(100.0));
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<EuropeanPut>(100.0));
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<DigitalCall>(100.0, 5.0));
    book.push_back(std::make_unique<Straddle>(100.0));
    for (double s : {90.0, 110.0}) {
        std::cout << "S=" << s << ":";
        for (const auto& p : book) std::cout << ' ' << (*p)(s);
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
}
Output:
S=90: 0 10 0 10
S=110: 10 0 5 10
Check by hand: at S=90 the call is 0 and the put is 10. At S=110 the call is 10, the put 0, the digital pays 5, and the straddle 10.
Interview trap: a virtual call per path per instrument is an indirect call inside the innermost loop. For speed, make the payoff a template parameter (the next-but-one card) or evaluate by type in batches.

front: A closed set of payoff types could be a virtual hierarchy or a std::variant. Show the variant version and state when each is preferred.
back:
Answer: A std::variant stores one of the listed types inline, with no vptr or heap allocation. std::visit dispatches over the listed types. This suits a closed set known at compile time. A virtual hierarchy suits an open set, such as plug-ins or types compiled separately.
#include <iostream>
#include <variant>
#include <vector>

struct Call { double k; };
struct Digital { double k, cash; };
using Payoff = std::variant<Call, Digital>;

struct Value {
    double s;
    double operator()(const Call& c) const { return s > c.k ? s - c.k : 0.0; }
    double operator()(const Digital& d) const { return s > d.k ? d.cash : 0.0; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Payoff> ps{Call{100.0}, Digital{100.0, 5.0}};
    for (const auto& p : ps) std::cout << std::visit(Value{110.0}, p) << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
10 5
Interview trap: the two designs trade in opposite directions. The variant makes adding an operation cheap and adding a type expensive, because every visitor must handle it. The virtual hierarchy is the reverse.

front: Why would a pricer use CRTP or a template parameter instead of a virtual pv() in its inner loop? Show the minimal CRTP and its output.
back:
Answer: The base's pv forwards to the derived type's pv_impl with a static_cast. The call is resolved at compile time and can be inlined, with no vtable. The cost is that there is no common base type, so a vector of different instruments needs another layer.
#include <iostream>

template <class Derived>
struct InstrumentCRTP {
    double pv(double df) const { return static_cast<const Derived*>(this)->pv_impl(df); }
};

struct Bond : InstrumentCRTP<Bond> {
    double face = 100.0;
    double pv_impl(double df) const { return face * df; }
};

int main() {
    Bond b;
    std::cout << b.pv(0.97) << '\n';     // resolved at compile time, no vtable
}
Output:
97
Interview trap: the static_cast<const Derived*> is safe only if the object really is a Derived. Passing a different type to the CRTP base is undefined behaviour and the compiler will not stop you.

front: Why does a class with a user-declared move constructor and deleted copy operations behave like std::unique_ptr? Predict the output of this program.
back:
Answer: Copies are deleted, so the object can only move. The move constructor transfers the id and leaves the source at -1, a valid state that is not a null state.
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

class Ticket {                          // move-only handle
public:
    explicit Ticket(int id) : id_(id) {}
    Ticket(const Ticket&) = delete;
    Ticket& operator=(const Ticket&) = delete;
    Ticket(Ticket&& o) noexcept : id_(std::exchange(o.id_, -1)) {}
    int id() const { return id_; }
private:
    int id_;
};

int main() {
    Ticket a{7};
    Ticket b = std::move(a);
    std::cout << a.id() << ' ' << b.id() << '\n';
}
Output:
-1 7
Interview trap: a moved-from object is only required to be valid, meaning destructible and assignable. Its value is unspecified. std::unique_ptr is stronger: a moved-from one is null by specification.

front: A struct holds a std::unique_ptr member. What does g++ say about Holder b = a;, and how do you fix it?
back:
Answer: The implicit copy constructor is deleted because a member cannot be copied. The fix depends on intent: move (Holder b = std::move(a);) if ownership transfers, or std::shared_ptr if it is shared.
g++ says:
snippet.cpp:9:16: error: use of deleted function ‘Holder::Holder(const Holder&)’
snippet.cpp:3:8: error: use of deleted function ‘std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>::unique_ptr(const std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>&) [with _Tp = int; _Dp = std::default_delete<int>]’
Interview trap: the struct is implicitly move-only. This is the rule of zero working for you. A Python object would silently share the reference, and the C++ compiler refuses the duplicate.

front: What does this program print, and why is the mutex free again after update(-1) throws?
back:
Answer: std::lock_guard locks in its constructor and unlocks in its destructor. Stack unwinding runs that destructor when the exception leaves update, so the lock is released.
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <stdexcept>

std::mutex m;

void update(int x) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);   // locks here
    if (x < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative");
    std::cout << "updated " << x << '\n';
}                                        // unlocks on normal return AND on throw

int main() {
    update(1);
    try { update(-1); }
    catch (const std::exception& e) { std::cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
    bool free_now = m.try_lock();
    std::cout << "mutex free after throw: " << free_now << '\n';
    if (free_now) m.unlock();
}
Output:
updated 1
caught: negative
mutex free after throw: 1
Interview trap: a manual m.lock() and m.unlock() pair leaks the lock on exception. Use lock_guard for a plain scope, or unique_lock when you need to unlock early.

front: Implement a scope-exit guard in C++ that runs a lambda at scope end unless it is dismissed. Show it used for rollback on an early return, and state the output.
back:
Answer: A template class stores the callable and runs it in its destructor unless dismiss() was called. Copying is deleted so that two guards cannot both run the same rollback. CTAD deduces the lambda type.
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

template <class F>
class ScopeExit {
    F f_;
    bool active_ = true;
public:
    explicit ScopeExit(F f) : f_(std::move(f)) {}
    ~ScopeExit() { if (active_) f_(); }
    ScopeExit(const ScopeExit&) = delete;
    ScopeExit& operator=(const ScopeExit&) = delete;
    void dismiss() { active_ = false; }
};

int book_trade(bool fail) {
    int stage = 0;
    ScopeExit rollback([&] { if (stage > 0) std::cout << "rollback from stage " << stage << '\n'; });
    stage = 1;                           // reserve capital
    if (fail) return -1;                 // early return: rollback still runs
    stage = 2;                           // post to ledger
    rollback.dismiss();
    return 0;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "result " << book_trade(true) << '\n';
    std::cout << "result " << book_trade(false) << '\n';
}
Output:
result rollback from stage 1
-1
result 0
The early return runs the rollback. The result prefix is printed before book_trade runs, because since C++17 the operands of << are sequenced left to right. The C++20 standard library has no built-in guard of this kind.
Interview trap: dismiss() on the success path is what makes the guard a rollback and not an unconditional cleanup.

front: A destructor throws while another exception is already unwinding the stack. What does this program print and why? Is a destructor noexcept by default?
back:
Answer: Yes. Destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11. ~Settlement is explicitly noexcept(false) here so that it can throw. While logic_error is in flight, the destructor throws a second exception, and the runtime calls std::terminate. The program aborts before the catch runs.
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Settlement {
    ~Settlement() noexcept(false) { throw std::runtime_error("settlement failed"); }
};

int main() {
    try {
        Settlement s;
        throw std::logic_error("trade rejected");
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
Output:
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::logic_error'
  what():  trade rejected
exit code -6Interview trap: a throw from a destructor is a hazard only during unwinding, but it is always poor design. Catch and log inside the destructor, or use a scope guard that does not throw.

front: std::move moves nothing by itself. It is a {{c1::cast to an rvalue reference}}, and the move is performed by the {{c2::move constructor or move assignment}} that overload resolution selects.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

class Ticket {                          // move-only handle
public:
    explicit Ticket(int id) : id_(id) {}
    Ticket(const Ticket&) = delete;
    Ticket& operator=(const Ticket&) = delete;
    Ticket(Ticket&& o) noexcept : id_(std::exchange(o.id_, -1)) {}
    int id() const { return id_; }
private:
    int id_;
};

int main() {
    Ticket a{7};
    Ticket b = std::move(a);
    std::cout << a.id() << ' ' << b.id() << '\n';
}
Output:
-1 7
Interview trap: std::move on a const object selects the copy constructor, because const T&& cannot bind to a move constructor taking T&&.
